analysis.one_liner: Toughens Clean Water Act enforcement with mandatory fines, more inspections, and public warnings at polluted waters.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in two House committees for a year and a half, got one subcommittee hearing in March 1994, and died without ever coming to a vote when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cracked down on facilities that hold Clean Water Act permits but keep violating them. It required warning signs at beaches and fishing spots where water is polluted or fish are unsafe to eat, forced sewage plants to tell customers about their own violations, set minimum penalties so fines could no longer fall below a polluter's savings, extended citizens' right to sue over past violations, and created a Clean Water Trust Fund from penalty money to pay for inspections and enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: People who swim, fish, or eat fish and shellfish from polluted waters, who would get warning signs and disclosure of violations; families living near contaminated waterways; and law-abiding facilities that currently compete against polluters who save money by breaking permit rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Swimmers, anglers, and communities near polluted water

how_it_helps.text: States must post visible signs at every major public access point to waters that violate quality standards or carry fish and shellfish consumption bans, including health effects and a phone number for more information.

Sewage treatment plants must tell every bill-paying customer about their permit violations over the past year, and industrial dischargers must post signs at facility entrances disclosing that they discharge pollutants into navigable waters.

Civil penalties must be at least as large as the economic benefit a violator gained from polluting, and serious or repeat violations carry mandatory minimum penalties of $1,000 to $5,000, addressing the bill's finding that penalties were often smaller than the savings from violating.

Citizens gain the right to sue over past violations, the 60-day notice window drops to 30 days, and EPA is directed to actively encourage citizen suits by sharing violator information and supporting the cases.

Significant violators become ineligible for new permits until violations are corrected, and the EPA Administrator must inspect every significant violator's facility and publish an annual list of them.

analysis.who_pays: Industrial and municipal facilities that discharge pollutants, through mandatory minimum fines, penalties that must cover their economic gain from violating, more frequent independent inspections, monthly monitoring reports, and disclosure requirements — costs that would be partly passed on to customers and ratepayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Facilities that discharge pollutants into waterways

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes significant compliance and paperwork costs on permitted facilities, including small and mid-size plants, through required inspections, monthly or quarterly monitoring reports signed by top officials, and uniform fish-sampling programs, and those costs are partly passed to customers.

Mandatory minimum penalties and a bar on compromising settlements below the violator's economic benefit remove the flexibility regulators currently have to resolve violations through cooperation rather than fines, which critics of strict enforcement argue can slow cleanup at difficult facilities.
Several provisions apply retroactively to pending cases, which raises fairness concerns for defendants facing new rules about litigation and penalties for conduct that predates the law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are direct and concrete for anyone who uses the nation's waters: you would learn when a beach is unsafe or fish are contaminated, and polluters could no longer treat fines as a cheap cost of doing business. The costs fall mainly on the facilities that discharge pollutants, partly passed to their customers, and the mandate-heavy design — minimum fines, less settlement flexibility, retroactivity — is aggressive and would have drawn legitimate pushback from regulated facilities and state agencies. On balance it is a consumer and public-health protection bill whose costs are borne by the regulated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and their subcommittees, got a hearing in March 1994, and expired at the end of the 103rd Congress in January 1995 without ever being reported out or voted on.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on July 23, 1993, and it was referred jointly to the Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee and the Public Works and Transportation Committee.
It was assigned to the Environment and Natural Resources subcommittee and the Water Resources and Environment subcommittee, and EPA was asked for its comments.
The Environment and Natural Resources subcommittee held a hearing on March 22, 1994, the only hearing the record shows.

The action history notes 'See H.R.3948' in March 1994, and the bill never advanced past subcommittee; no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that discharge pollutants into waterways came out ahead: they continued operating under the existing enforcement system without mandatory minimum penalties, economic-benefit recovery, new inspections, or public disclosure of their violations.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Members who added their names in March 1994 such as Reps. Shays and Machtley (R) and Sanders (I).

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the record shows only sponsorship: 43 of the 49 cosponsors were Democrats, with 5 Republicans and 1 Independent — substantial but predominantly Democratic support, and no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Industrial dischargers (chemical plants, factories, and other permitted polluters)
industries.note: The bill would have required penalties at least equal to what violators saved by polluting, minimum fines for serious and repeat violations, annual independent inspections, monthly monitoring reports, and a permit ban for significant violators — ending the situation the bill itself documents, where fines were often smaller than the profit from violating. Its interest ran directly against the public's interest in knowing about and stopping pollution.

Utilities would have gained federal authority to inspect and fine industrial users of their systems and a federal backstop when state permits expire, but would also have had to list their own permit violations in every quarterly customer bill and post discharge notices. Municipal stormwater discharges were exempted from the sign requirements.

The bill expanded citizen suits to past violations, shortened the notice period, barred state actions from blocking citizen enforcement, and directed EPA to supply information and support to citizen groups bringing cases. Over the prior four years citizen suits had recovered $9 million in penalties for the Treasury.
